main.title: SingStar
main.subtitle: A microphone turns listening into a game
main.summary: SingStar is London Studio's PlayStation 2 karaoke game, introduced in Europe in May 2004. Players sing along to familiar recordings using USB microphones while the game measures their performance. Lyrics and pitch guidance make the song visible, allowing the television to become the centre of a shared singing session. The red and blue microphones give two people an immediate role in front of the screen. The idea depends less on learning an unusual controller than on choosing a song somebody already knows and giving them a reason to sing it aloud.

cards.heading: A microphone turns listening into a game
cards.text: SingStar is London Studio's PlayStation 2 karaoke game, introduced in Europe in May 2004. Players sing along to familiar recordings using USB microphones while the game measures their performance. Lyrics and pitch guidance make the song visible, allowing the television to become the centre of a shared singing session. The red and blue microphones give two people an immediate role in front of the screen. The idea depends less on learning an unusual controller than on choosing a song somebody already knows and giving them a reason to sing it aloud.

cards.heading: Follow the line, then pass the microphone
cards.text: The display connects the words to a guide for the notes, giving feedback while the recording continues. Scoring turns a familiar song into a challenge that can be repeated or shared with another singer. The microphone makes performance visible in a different way from pressing a button: the player's own voice becomes the input. A gathering can move from watching someone else to taking part as soon as a microphone changes hands. That simple transition helped the game fit into social occasions where people had very different levels of experience with games.

cards.heading: A song library grows around the hardware
cards.text: Later editions expanded the available music and produced regional releases for different audiences. Camera support also allowed singers to see and record themselves, connecting the performance to the room around the console. The series continued on PlayStation 3 and PlayStation 4, where online song purchases enlarged its library. Those services closed in January 2020 while existing offline content remained accessible. The original PlayStation 2 game established the essential arrangement: a recording, a readable guide and two microphones that invited the people beside the television to become the entertainment.

main.title: RalliSport Challenge 2
main.subtitle: Rally takes several different roads
main.summary: RalliSport Challenge 2 is Digital Illusions CE's Xbox racing game, released in North America on 4 May 2004. It expands the earlier RalliSport Challenge through a career that moves between rally stages, rallycross, hill climbs and other forms of competition. Snow, ice and night driving change the conditions around the car, while different event formats ask for different habits. A solitary run against the clock demands a clean line; a race with opponents adds the problem of sharing it. The sequel makes that variety the structure of its championship.

cards.heading: Rally takes several different roads
cards.text: RalliSport Challenge 2 is Digital Illusions CE's Xbox racing game, released in North America on 4 May 2004. It expands the earlier RalliSport Challenge through a career that moves between rally stages, rallycross, hill climbs and other forms of competition. Snow, ice and night driving change the conditions around the car, while different event formats ask for different habits. A solitary run against the clock demands a clean line; a race with opponents adds the problem of sharing it. The sequel makes that variety the structure of its championship.

cards.heading: The car remembers the collision
cards.text: Damage can remove body panels and affect the way a car performs, turning an untidy corner into a problem that continues beyond the impact. Tuning options allow tyres, gearing and other settings to be adjusted for the conditions ahead. The player can therefore prepare for a surface as well as react to it. Career progress unlocks more cars and courses, while time attacks offer a simpler reason to return to a familiar stage. Better results come from understanding where a particular car has grip and where it needs restraint.

cards.heading: A racing club beyond the console
cards.text: The game formed part of Microsoft's XSN Sports range, combining Xbox Live competition with online rankings and tournament features. System Link and local multiplayer offered other ways to race, with online sessions supporting larger groups than split-screen play. Reviewers praised the presentation, accessible handling and variety, making it one of the original Xbox's best-regarded racing games. The original Live service ended in 2010, but the single-player career retains the breadth of its design. Its changing surfaces and event types make the championship a continuing lesson in adapting to the road.

main.title: Red Dead Revolver
main.subtitle: An arcade western before Redemption
main.summary: Rockstar dates the first release of Red Dead Revolver for PlayStation 2 and Xbox to May 3, 2004.

cards.heading: An arcade western before Redemption
cards.text: Rockstar dates Red Dead Revolver's first release on PlayStation 2 and Xbox to May 3, 2004. Linear chapters lead through shootouts, duels and exaggerated characters inspired by Italian westerns, comics and arcade games. Dead Eye slows the action for deliberate aiming, establishing a mechanic that later Red Dead games would expand. Strong colour, music and caricature give this early entry its pulp identity.

cards.heading: Angel Studios becomes Rockstar San Diego
cards.text: The project began at Angel Studios in association with Capcom. Rockstar acquired the studio and changed the game's direction during its long development. Separate scenarios, strongly defined bosses and arcade-style action remained alongside a new emphasis on western imagery and editing. That mixed production history helps explain the form of the finished game.

cards.heading: Dead Eye plans the shots
cards.text: Dead Eye slows time so the player can mark targets before releasing a rapid sequence of shots. It translates the speed of a western gunslinger into a controllable pause for planning. Aiming and timing combine in one burst of action, with spectacular precision available through the system. Later games would retain and develop this central mechanic.

cards.heading: A western in separate chapters
cards.text: Separate chapters let each stage introduce another setting and antagonist. Strong colours, caricatured figures and music associated with Italian western cinema support the succession of scenes. Redemption would later connect related imagery to a larger, more naturalistic frontier. Revolver's compact encounters preserve a more openly arcade interpretation of the western.

main.title: Mario vs. Donkey Kong
main.summary: Mario vs. Donkey Kong brings Nintendo’s rivalry to a puzzle-platform game on Game Boy Advance. Its design follows the compact challenges of the 1994 Game Boy Donkey Kong.

cards.text: Mario vs. Donkey Kong is a 2004 puzzle-platform game developed by Nintendo Software Technology and published by Nintendo for the Game Boy Advance. The game is the spiritual successor to Donkey Kong, which was released in 1994 for the Game Boy.
The gameplay revolves around a combination of platform and puzzle elements. Players control Mario through small sets of challenges to find a key and rescue Mini-Marios from Donkey Kong.

Mario vs. Donkey Kong received positive reviews, particularly for its gameplay and graphics. It spawned a franchise of the same name with the first sequel, Mario vs. Donkey Kong 2: March of the Minis, released on Nintendo DS in September 2006. A remake for the Nintendo Switch was released in February 2024.

main.title: DRIV3R
main.subtitle: Driving and gunplay across three cities
main.summary: On June 21, 2004 Reflections and Atari released DRIV3R in North America for PlayStation 2 and Xbox.

cards.heading: Driving and gunplay across three cities
cards.text: On June 21, 2004 Reflections and Atari released DRIV3R in North America for PlayStation 2 and Xbox. After two games centered on the car, the third entry attempts to merge chases, on-foot exploration and larger cities. Its ambition also exposes the difficulties of the generation: simulating traffic, physics, missions and open spaces means distributing technical resources and player attention across systems that do not always have the same precision.

cards.heading: Driving through three cities
cards.text: Undercover supplies the story missions, Take A Ride allows free exploration, and Driving Games offers vehicle challenges. Across the three cities, players can change vehicles, damage them and attract police attention through unlawful actions. A notoriety system changes the pursuit as offences accumulate. Mission-critical vehicles must survive, making their condition part of the objective.

cards.heading: Leaving the car and entering combat
cards.text: Driver 3 introduces new gameplay mechanics to existing ones including motorbikes and speedboats, swimming, a health bar, and gun combat. Alongside being arrested by the cops or failing objectives in story mode, players can also fail if they run out of health without finding first aid kits to recover it. Combat focuses on the use of guns, based on real-life models and featuring a mixture of pistols, shotguns, assault rifles and sub-machine guns, and grenade launchers, to take down enemies; all weapons have a limit on ammo except for the lead character's personal weapon, but more can be found from dealing with enemies, or around the game world in Take A Ride.

cards.heading: Missions, free roaming and replay editing
cards.text: Undercover missions involve escaping pursuers, reaching places or taking down targets, sometimes within a time limit. Take A Ride opens Miami, Nice and Istanbul for exploration and secrets, including special cars and the hostile Timmy Vermicelli characters. The replay editor supplies different camera angles and effects, letting players shape a limited recording of their own driving into a short sequence.

cards.heading: Tanner follows a car-smuggling ring
cards.text: Driver 3 (stylized as DRIV3R) is a 2004 action-adventure game, the third installment in the Driver series. It was developed by Reflections Interactive, published by Atari, and released on PlayStation 2, Xbox and mobile phones in June 2004, Microsoft Windows in March 2005, and Game Boy Advance in October 2005. The game's story focuses on players assuming the role of John Tanner, an undercover FBI agent, as he investigates a car-smuggling ring across three countries, in order to identify and arrest its boss and learn who they are planning to sell a cache of stolen cars to. The game expanded upon its predecessors with on-foot sections, gun combat, and drive-by shooting, with virtual recreations of three major cities - Miami, Nice, and Istanbul - free-roam game mode, and an improvement to the series' film-making "director mode".

cards.heading: Driving praised, on-foot action criticised
cards.text: Driver 3 was a much-hyped and anticipated title, and although the game was a commercial success, it received mixed reviews upon release, except for the PC edition which received negative feedback from critics. While the graphics, story and driving were praised, criticism was focused on the on foot controls, awkward shooting mechanics, and performance issues, with some critics accusing Atari of rushing the game's release to avoid competing with Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas later that year. Some publications referred to the game as disastrous. The game was succeeded by Driver: Parallel Lines (2006), before being followed up by a direct sequel, Driver: San Francisco, in 2011.

main.title: Spider-Man 2
main.summary: Spider-Man 2 is a 2004 action-adventure game based on the 2004 film of the same name.

cards.text: Spider-Man 2 is a 2004 action-adventure game based on the 2004 film of the same name. The game is the sequel to 2002's Spider-Man, itself based on the 2002 film of the same name. It was released on June 29, 2004, for the PlayStation 2, GameCube, Xbox, Microsoft Windows, and Game Boy Advance, followed by N-Gage and Nintendo DS versions later the same year. A PlayStation Portable version was released almost one year later, on March 23, 2005. The Game Boy Advance version, developed by Digital Eclipse, was re-released on a twin pack cartridge and bundled with that system's version of the 2002 Spider-Man game in 2005. A tie-in game, titled Spider-Man 2: Activity Center, was also released in June 2004. Published by Activision, the console versions were developed by Treyarch, while the others had different developers and are drastically different as a result.

All game versions closely follow the film's plot, but expand upon it by including scenes and characters that do not appear in the film. Set 2 years after the events of Spider-Man, the game finds Peter Parker struggling to manage both his personal life and his duties as Spider-Man. When scientist and Peter's mentor, Otto Octavius, becomes the diabolical villain Doctor Octopus after an accident, Spider-Man must stop him from recreating a dangerous fusion power experiment.

The game's console versions were positively received, with critics commending the realistic Manhattan setting and web-swinging mechanics. The handheld versions received mixed reviews, while the PC version received negative reviews. The game was followed by Spider-Man 3, itself based on the 2007 film of the same name.

main.title: Shin Megami Tensei: Digital Devil Saga
main.summary: Shin Megami Tensei: Digital Devil Saga is a duology of role-playing video games developed by Atlus for the PlayStation 2.

cards.text: Shin Megami Tensei: Digital Devil Saga is a duology of role-playing video games developed by Atlus for the PlayStation 2. They are a spin-off of the Megami Tensei series. The first Digital Devil Saga was released in Japan in 2004, North America in 2005, and Europe in 2006. Its direct sequel, Shin Megami Tensei: Digital Devil Saga 2, released in 2005 in Japan and North America, and 2007 in Europe and Australasia. The games were published in Europe and Australasia by Ghostlight and in other regions by Atlus and its North American subsidiary Atlus USA.

Digital Devil Saga follows the Embryon, a tribe who fights against five other tribes in a digital world called the Junkyard. After being infected with a demon virus that grants them demonic powers, the Embryon must fight with and devour the other tribes to ascend to "Nirvana". During the conflict, they shelter a woman named Sera, who has the power to calm their demonic powers. In Digital Devil Saga 2, having escaped into the devastated real world, the Embryon are caught up in the fight against the Karma Society, who are intimately linked to the source of the disaster. The gameplay of both titles features third-person navigation of playable characters around to-scale environments, and turn-based gameplay against demonic monsters and human enemies.

Digital Devil Saga began development pre-2002 under the working title New Goddess. The game's concept and original draft were written by Japanese author Yu Godai, who collaborated with Atlus scriptwriter Tadashi Satomi until withdrawing from the project for health issues. The gameplay concept of characters transforming into demons was based on an unused idea for Shin Megami Tensei. The second game began development immediately after the first, with the main development effort going into refining and improving the gameplay. While their commercial performances varied, both games were heavily praised by critics for their story, graphics and gameplay. Since release, the game has inspired a mobile prequel, and Godai wrote a series of novels based on her original premise for the story.

main.title: Sudeki
main.summary: Sudeki is a 2004 action role-playing game developed by Climax Studios.

cards.text: Sudeki is a 2004 action role-playing game developed by Climax Studios. It was originally released for Xbox by Microsoft Game Studios. A Microsoft Windows port was released in Europe by Zoo Digital Publishing in 2005, and worldwide via Steam and GOG.com in 2014 by Climax. Set on the splintered world of Sudeki, divided into the twin planets Illumina and Akloria, the storyline follows four characters chosen by the god Tetsu to prevent the return of the dark god Haigou and reform Sudeki. Gameplay follows the four protagonists as they explore various environments, with different characters fighting enemies using third-person melee or first-person shooter combat.

The concept of the game began in 1999, originally as a Dreamcast project. After multiple platform changes, production proper started in 2000 as an Xbox exclusive. As Climax's first role-playing game, the team wanted to emulate Japanese RPGs, though the art style was adjusted from its earlier anime-inspired aesthetic to appeal to a Western audience. The game saw mixed reviews from journalists; praise went to its graphics and combat system, but there were mixed thoughts on the narrative due to its pacing and generic content. It also met with low sales in all release regions.

main.title: Boktai 2: Solar Boy Django
main.subtitle: The solar hunter returns home
main.summary: Boktai 2: Solar Boy Django is Konami's Game Boy Advance action role-playing sequel bringing Django back to San Miguel. A vampire steals the Gun Del Sol, leaving the returning hunter to find another way of fighting while investigating what has happened to his home. The cartridge retains the light sensor that connects real sunlight with the adventure's resources. The new situation changes how that central idea is used, giving a familiar hero a reason to learn different equipment before he can recover the weapon that defined his first journey through the darkness.

cards.heading: The solar hunter returns home
cards.text: Boktai 2: Solar Boy Django is Konami's Game Boy Advance action role-playing sequel bringing Django back to San Miguel. A vampire steals the Gun Del Sol, leaving the returning hunter to find another way of fighting while investigating what has happened to his home. The cartridge retains the light sensor that connects real sunlight with the adventure's resources. The new situation changes how that central idea is used, giving a familiar hero a reason to learn different equipment before he can recover the weapon that defined his first journey through the darkness.

cards.heading: The sunlight moves into another weapon
cards.text: Zazie gives Django the Sol de Vice, a glove capable of imbuing ordinary weapons with solar power. A sword can therefore become part of the same relationship between daylight and the undead that previously centred on the gun. The change broadens the physical form of combat while keeping the sensor relevant to preparation. Django's new tools need to be understood on their own terms, making the loss of his original weapon a practical change to the adventure rather than only a story event that leaves the player's available actions untouched.

cards.heading: The town gives the investigation a centre
cards.text: San Miguel provides the setting for Django's search for answers, including the disappearance of the blacksmith Smith and reports of the vampire passing through. Following these leads connects individual expeditions with the condition of a place the protagonist already knows. The solar sensor keeps the surrounding real world involved while the town supplies a more personal reason to continue. The sequel builds on the original game's unusual cartridge through that changed context, giving daylight another set of weapons to power and giving the hunter a home whose problems make the next journey worth undertaking.

main.title: Gradius V
main.subtitle: The Vic Viper returns
main.summary: Gradius V is Treasure's PlayStation 2 scrolling shooter, published by Konami and first released in Japan on 22 July 2004. The Vic Viper travels through Bacterian territory, fighting enemy formations, large machines and hazards that fill the route ahead. Three-dimensional graphics support action played mainly on a two-dimensional plane. Open stretches alternate with narrow passages and changes of scrolling direction, asking the player to read the surroundings as carefully as the incoming fire. A second player can join the same screen for simultaneous cooperative play.

cards.heading: The Vic Viper returns
cards.text: Gradius V is Treasure's PlayStation 2 scrolling shooter, published by Konami and first released in Japan on 22 July 2004. The Vic Viper travels through Bacterian territory, fighting enemy formations, large machines and hazards that fill the route ahead. Three-dimensional graphics support action played mainly on a two-dimensional plane. Open stretches alternate with narrow passages and changes of scrolling direction, asking the player to read the surroundings as carefully as the incoming fire. A second player can join the same screen for simultaneous cooperative play.

cards.heading: Shape the formation around the ship
cards.text: Collecting capsules advances the familiar power-up selection, letting the player decide when to activate speed, weapons or additional support. The Options accompanying the Vic Viper add more firing positions, and different weapon configurations change how they can be controlled. Holding or arranging that fire allows an attack to reach enemies while the main ship stays elsewhere. The important choice is therefore not simply which weapon is strongest: it is how its pattern fits the space, enemy positions and safe route through a particular encounter.

cards.heading: Learning the route through repetition
cards.text: A collision costs a life, but the game can allow an immediate return at the point of defeat instead of always sending the player back to a checkpoint. Stage selection and score-focused play provide ways to revisit the route. Treasure's experience with demanding shooters appears in the changing layouts and carefully organised enemy patterns. Hitoshi Sakimoto supplied the score, while Hidetaka Tenjin created the cover illustration. Reviewers praised the level design and presentation, alongside warnings about the difficulty that remained central to mastering its stages.
